subjective.question: Define language according to Sapir.
subjective.answer: Sapir (1921) defines language as "a purely human and non-instinctive method of communicating ideas, emotions and desires by means of voluntarily produced symbols."

subjective.question: Write down the functions of language given by Jakobson.
subjective.answer: Jakobson (1960) describes six functions of language: (1) Referential — oriented to the context, for conveying information; (2) Emotive/Expressive — oriented to the addresser, expressing feelings and attitudes; (3) Conative — oriented to the addressee, e.g. commands and requests; (4) Phatic — concerned with establishing and maintaining social contact ('small talk'); (5) Metalingual — language used to talk about language itself; (6) Poetic — focused on the message for its own sake, e.g. in literature.

subjective.question: Write the functions of language given by Halliday.
subjective.answer: Halliday's functional grammar views language from a socio-cultural perspective, as a system of meanings. He proposed three metafunctions of language: (1) Ideational — language used to organize the speaker's or writer's experience of the real or imagined world; (2) Interpersonal — language used to establish and maintain social relations; (3) Textual — language used to organize the text itself so that it forms a coherent message.

subjective.question: Define the terms 'productivity' and 'duality' as features of human language.
subjective.answer: Productivity: Humans continually create new expressions and novel utterances by manipulating their linguistic resources to describe new objects and situations. The potential number of utterances in any human language is infinite, unlike the communication systems of other creatures. Duality: Human language is organized at two levels simultaneously. At one level we have distinct sounds (e.g. n, b, i), and at another level we have different combinations of these sounds carrying distinct meanings (e.g. bin, nib).

subjective.question: What is displacement as a feature of human language?
subjective.answer: Displacement is the property of human language that allows users to talk about things and events not present in the immediate environment. Animal communication cannot effectively be used to relate events that are far removed in time and place, whereas humans can refer to past and future time and to things that are not present here and now.

subjective.question: Write down the main characteristics of an international language.
subjective.answer: An international language: (1) is spoken by a lot of people of different nationalities; (2) its speakers do not need to assume the culture of the said language; (3) its ownership is denationalized; (4) the goal of its education is to enable learners to communicate their ideas and culture to others across the world; (5) it is spread not only by its people migrating to other areas but by the people of other areas acquiring it; and (6) its special role is recognized by almost every country, either by making it an official language or by requiring its study as a foreign language.

subjective.question: Name the different periods of English language development.
subjective.answer: The history of English is usually divided into five periods: (1) Pre-Old English — the period of tribal dialects (tribes such as the Jutes, Saxons and Angles); (2) Old English (from the 8th century) — the period of full inflections, in which English was written with the runic alphabet borrowed from the Anglo-Saxons; (3) Middle English (1100-1500) — the period of levelled inflections, in which French became the language of power and English the language of the common people; (4) Early Modern English (1500-1800) — the period of lost inflections, marked by the printing press, the Renaissance and the colonization of America; (5) Later Modern English (1800 to the present) — the period of scientific development, industrialization, colonization and the internet, in which English became the language of science, technology and international communication.

subjective.question: What is Kachru's Three Circles model of English? Name three countries of the Inner Circle.
subjective.answer: Kachru (1985) presented the spread of English in terms of three concentric circles. The Inner Circle represents the traditional bases of English — countries where English is the primary/mother language; these are norm-providing. The Outer Circle represents countries where English has an important official/institutional role as a second language (former British colonies); these are norm-developing. The Expanding Circle represents countries where English is taught as a foreign language; these are norm-dependent. Three Inner Circle countries are Australia, New Zealand and Ireland (also anglophone Canada, South Africa, the UK and the USA).

subjective.question: Write a note on the status of English in Pakistan.
subjective.answer: English enjoys a very important status in Pakistan. Although Urdu is the national language, English is used as an official language in government, law, the military, business, media and education. It is a compulsory subject in schools and the medium of instruction in higher education and for science and technical subjects. English may have a small number of proficient speakers in Pakistan, but these are very influential people. Proficiency in English is a primary condition for obtaining better jobs, and success in prestigious professions is heavily dependent on English language competence.

subjective.question: Summarize the place of English in the different education policies of Pakistan.
subjective.answer: Education Policy 1959: primary and secondary education in Urdu and higher education in English; the national language was to gradually replace English by 1974. Education Policy 1969: Urdu was declared the official language in West Pakistan and Bengali in East Pakistan. Education Policy 1970: linked the change of medium of instruction at higher level with the replacement of English for official purposes. Constitution of 1973: endorsed that Urdu should be used for official purposes within fifteen years, with promotion of Arabic, English and provincial languages. National Education Policy 1979: recommended 'Islamization and Urduisation' at every level; English was dubbed a legacy of colonialism. Education Policy 1989: made English a compulsory subject from grade one. Education Policy 1992: recommended English as the medium of instruction for science and technical subjects at tertiary level. Education Policy 2009: emphasized the promotion of English as a compulsory subject from grade 1 upwards, with Mathematics and Science to be taught in English from grade four onwards.

subjective.question: How is English a language of power and prestige in South Asia?
subjective.answer: In South Asia, English was never seriously questioned as the language of power. South Asian governments generally teach most children through the vernacular languages while reserving English for the elite. The English-using elite are considered politically more liberal, democratic and tolerant, and the English divide is contingent upon the distribution of power rather than a free choice of the medium of education. From the 1970s onwards, South Asian countries shifted from teaching English through its literature and grammar to ELT (EFL/ESL), which brought the realization that non-native South Asian varieties of English should be recognized not merely as 'incorrect' Englishes but as legitimate alternatives.

subjective.question: What is the difference between a native speaker and a non-native speaker?
subjective.answer: A native speaker is a person who speaks a particular language since he/she was a baby, rather than having learned it as a child or adult. A non-native speaker is a person who has another native tongue other than the language being used. However, this distinction is often criticized: in many cases the categorization of speakers into native/non-native has a non-linguistic basis (e.g. race, colour), ELT institutions still largely prefer Western teachers of English, and native-speakerism remains the dominant ideology in much of ELT.

subjective.question: What is psycholinguistics? Write its scope.
subjective.answer: Psycholinguistics explores the relationship between the human mind and language. It treats the language user as an individual rather than a representative of a society, whose linguistic performance is determined by the strengths and limitations of mental processes. It establishes an understanding of the language process, examines language as a product of the human mind, and traces similar patterns of linguistic behaviour across large groups. It draws on ideas and knowledge from associated areas such as neurolinguistics, phonetics and semantics. Its six major areas are: language processing, language storage and access, comprehension theory, language and the brain, language in exceptional circumstances, and first language acquisition.

subjective.question: Briefly describe the stages of language development in children.
subjective.answer: Birth: the child makes vegetative sounds — crying, burping and sucking noises. 6 weeks: cooing starts. 16 weeks: laughing starts. 16 weeks to 6 months: vocal play — speech-like sounds; vowels emerge before consonants. 6-9 months: babbling — distinguished from vocal play by the presence of true syllables (consonants plus vowels), often repeated. 10-11 months: first words are produced, forming single-word utterances. 18 months: a rapid explosion in vocabulary size; two-word sentences emerge and children show telegraphic speech, learning about 40 new words a week. 2 years 6 months: increasingly complex sentences are produced. Grammatical development carries on throughout childhood, and we never stop learning new words.

subjective.question: What are lexical entries, lexical storage and lexical access?
subjective.answer: Lexical entries concern the information we need to store in our mind about lexical items (their form, meaning and grammatical behaviour). Lexical storage concerns how lexical items are stored in relation to each other in the mental lexicon. Lexical access is the process that enables us to retrieve lexical items from storage when we need them in speaking, listening, reading or writing.

subjective.question: What is Second Language Acquisition (SLA)? Also write its scope.
subjective.answer: SLA has two interpretations. In general terms, it describes learning a second language. More specifically, it is the theory of the process by which we acquire a second language — mainly a subconscious process during communication — and the scientific discipline devoted to studying that process. The additional language is called a second language (L2), even though it may actually be the third, fourth or tenth to be acquired; it is also called the target language (TL). The scope of SLA includes: informal L2 learning in naturalistic contexts; formal L2 learning in classrooms; and L2 learning that involves a mixture of these settings.

subjective.question: What is behaviourism? How does it explain language learning?
subjective.answer: Behaviourism views language learning as the formation of habits, similar to any other kind of learning. It is based on the notions of stimulus and response: human beings are exposed to numerous stimuli in their environment, and the response they give to a stimulus will be reinforced if successful, that is, if some desired outcome is obtained. Applied to language, acquisition involves habit formation through the process of Stimulus-Response-Reinforcement (S-R-R).

subjective.question: Write the criticism of Contrastive Analysis.
subjective.answer: Contrastive Analysis (CA) has been criticized on three main grounds: (1) it cannot explain how learners know more than they have heard or have been taught; (2) CA analyses were not always validated by evidence, and they also missed many learner errors — not all errors are caused by L1 interference; (3) instructional materials produced according to this approach are language-specific, so they cannot be used for learners of different first languages.

subjective.question: What is interlanguage? Write some common misconceptions about it.
subjective.answer: Interlanguage (Selinker, 1972) is the intermediate state (interim grammar) of a learner's language as it moves towards the target L2. It is a third language system in its own right which differs from both L1 and L2, and its development is a creative process influenced by both. Common misconceptions are: that interlanguage is merely a collection of errors rather than a systematic grammar; that it is simply the result of L1 interference; that it is static, whereas it develops continuously; and that every learner's interlanguage will automatically reach target-language norms, whereas fossilization may stop its development.

subjective.question: Write down Krashen's five hypotheses of second language acquisition.
subjective.answer: Krashen's Monitor Model consists of five hypotheses: (1) Acquisition-Learning Hypothesis — acquisition is a subconscious process, while learning is conscious knowledge of rules; (2) Monitor Hypothesis — what is 'learned' is available only as a monitor, for editing or making changes to what has already been produced; (3) Natural Order Hypothesis — grammatical structures are acquired in a predictable order; (4) Input Hypothesis — learners progress by receiving comprehensible input slightly beyond their current level (i+1); (5) Affective Filter Hypothesis — emotional factors such as motivation, confidence and anxiety can raise or lower a 'filter' that blocks or allows input to be acquired.

subjective.question: What is Universal Grammar (UG)?
subjective.answer: Universal Grammar is the set of universal principles that form part of the mental representation of language. It is this mental grammar that mediates between the sound and meaning of language. The properties of the human mind are what make languages universal: what all languages have in common is UG. UG is assumed to be the guiding force of child language acquisition, explaining how children acquire linguistic competence — knowledge far richer than the input they receive (the logical problem of language learning).

subjective.question: Write a detailed note on the Grammar Translation Method (GTM).
subjective.answer: GTM, also known as the classical method, is one of the oldest methods; in the early 1500s it was used for teaching Latin and Greek, and it was popular in foreign-language classrooms from the mid-19th to the mid-20th century. Basic assumptions: a foreign language can easily be learnt through translation; grammar is the soul of language; learning foreign languages is part of a truly liberal education; the structure of the foreign language can best be taught by comparing it with L1. Goals: to learn a language in order to read its literature; to be able to translate from one language to another; L1 is maintained as the reference system in L2 learning. Practices: words are taught through bilingual word lists and dictionaries; grammar is taught deductively — rules are presented and studied in an organized way and then practised through translation exercises. A GTM lesson includes a reading passage, comprehension questions, antonyms/synonyms, cognates, grammar exercises, using words in sentences, memorization, composition and summarizing. Criticism: it is teacher-centred and aims at accuracy, not fluency; it does not cater for the communicative aspect of language; and it overemphasizes language as a mass of rules and vocabulary to be memorized and translated.

subjective.question: Write a note on the Bilingual Method.
subjective.answer: In the Bilingual Method, the mother tongue is used only by the teacher, not by the students. The teacher uses L1 to explain the meanings of words and sentences, while students practise speaking in the target language. Its major advantage is saving time: explaining in the mother tongue is quick and exact, so more time can be given to practice. It emphasizes speech practice and pattern practice without the lengthy explanations of the Grammar Translation Method.

subjective.question: What is the difference between the Silent Way and the Bilingual Method?
subjective.answer: In the Silent Way, the teacher remains largely silent and learners are encouraged to discover the language themselves, whereas in the Bilingual Method the teacher actively explains meanings using the mother tongue. In the Bilingual Method, the mother tongue is used by the teacher only; in the Silent Way, the mother tongue is generally avoided. The Silent Way emphasizes learner autonomy and discovery learning, while the Bilingual Method emphasizes time-saving explanation followed by speech practice.

subjective.question: Write any two roles of the teacher in a Communicative Language Teaching (CLT) classroom.
subjective.answer: In a CLT classroom the teacher acts as: (1) a facilitator of the communication process, who sets up communicative activities and helps learners communicate effectively rather than dominating the class; and (2) a guide/manager and needs analyst, who organizes group and pair work, monitors learners' performance, and provides feedback and support according to learners' communicative needs.

subjective.question: Write down the stages of listening.
subjective.answer: Listening involves five stages: (1) Receiving — the response caused by sound waves stimulating the sensory receptors of the ear; we receive the words while we hear. (2) Understanding — learning what the speaker means: the thoughts and emotions behind the message. (3) Remembering — adding the message to the mind's storage box; as our attention is selective, what is remembered may be different from what was originally heard. (4) Evaluating — judging the message in some way, e.g. the speaker's intentions or motives, even without conscious awareness. (5) Responding — verbal and/or non-verbal feedback determines whether a message has been received and tells about the degree of success in communication.

subjective.question: Write the disadvantages of using audio-visual aids in teaching listening.
subjective.answer: The disadvantages of audio-visual aids are: (1) they reduce the teacher's role in the classroom; (2) students can develop a lazy attitude and take the lesson less seriously; (3) films and pictures may present an oversimplified version of the world; and (4) students may take time to get used to them, as they see them as a source of entertainment rather than learning.

subjective.question: What are Harmer's principles for teaching listening?
subjective.answer: Harmer (2001) gives the following principles for teaching listening: (1) encourage students to listen as often and as much as possible; (2) help students prepare to listen; (3) once may not be enough — students should be allowed to listen more than once; (4) encourage students to respond to the content of the listening text, not just to its language; (5) different listening stages demand different listening tasks; and (6) good teachers exploit listening texts to the full.

subjective.question: What is unidirectional (one-way) listening?
subjective.answer: Unidirectional listening is the second mode of communicative listening, in which the listening is one-way. The auditory input surrounds us as we move through the day and comes from a variety of sources: overheard conversations, public announcements, recorded messages, instructional situations of all kinds, and public performances. As we hear speakers but are unable to interact with them, we often talk to ourselves in a reactive or self-dialogue manner as we analyse what we hear.

subjective.question: Write the techniques/activities for developing speaking skills.
subjective.answer: Widely used categories of speaking activities include: (1) Early activities — students getting acquainted with each other in a realistic context, 'Two Minute Conversations' (Wong, 1994), and structured interviews using wh- and yes/no questions. (2) Acting from a script — students act out scenes from plays or course books, or dialogues they have written themselves; the teacher works like a theatre director, drawing attention to stress, intonation and speed; it builds confidence and contextualizes language. (3) Communication games — information-gap games (solving a puzzle, drawing a picture, putting things in order, finding similarities/differences) and television/radio games such as 'twenty questions', which provide good fluency practice. (4) Prepared talks/speeches — a student makes a presentation on a topic of his/her own choice, speaking from notes rather than a script, with time to prepare and rehearse; listeners may be given responsibilities such as peer evaluation, and videotaping allows in-depth critique later. Modern practice has shifted from accuracy-focused drills to more authentic communication activities.

subjective.question: What is the difference between planned and unplanned speaking?
subjective.answer: Planned speaking is speech that is prepared in advance, such as a lesson or a wedding speech, where the speaker has time to organize content, language and delivery. Unplanned speaking is spontaneous speech that takes place without preparation, such as a conversation that happens when we bump into someone on the street.

subjective.question: What is reading? Also write the strategies for extensive reading.
subjective.answer: Reading is a fluent process of readers combining information from a text and their own background knowledge to build meaning. The goal of reading is comprehension. Instructors aim to produce students who can use reading strategies to maximize their comprehension of text, identify relevant and non-relevant information, and tolerate less than word-by-word comprehension. Two strategies for extensive reading are: (1) keep a reading journal/diary in which students record their response to a book, e.g. notes on characters and events, or their personal reaction to a story or topic; (2) survey the books read by the whole class and put a star or sticker against the titles of books they liked, so that other students can use these recommendations when choosing their next book.

subjective.question: What is skimming?
subjective.answer: Skimming is a reading strategy in which the reader makes a quick survey of the text to get the main idea, identify the text structure, and confirm or question predictions. It is also used to skim a text for specific information, e.g. to answer true/false statements or to fill gaps, without reading every word carefully.

subjective.question: What are the types of tasks used in teaching reading?
subjective.answer: Three types of tasks are used in teaching reading: (1) Slashed/cut-up texts — a text is cut into pieces (e.g. paragraphs or sentences) and students put them back into the correct order. (2) Jigsaw reading — a text is divided into parts; different students/groups read different parts and then share information to reconstruct the whole text. (3) Running and reading — texts are placed around the classroom (e.g. on walls); students move around, read them and complete a task, which adds a physical, game-like element to reading.

subjective.question: Write the characteristics of a good reader.
subjective.answer: Individual differences impact reading processing, and a good reader is characterized by factors such as: working memory capacity; the understandings stored in long-term memory (background knowledge); language ability; and clear goals for reading. Good readers also read extensively, use a flexible reading style suited to their purpose, and integrate information in the text with their existing knowledge.

subjective.question: Write a note on the process and product approaches to teaching writing.
subjective.answer: In the teaching of writing we can focus either on the product of writing or on the writing process itself. When concentrating on the product, we are only interested in the aim of the task and in the end product (e.g. the genre approach). The process approach pays attention to the various stages that any piece of writing goes through: by spending time with learners on pre-writing phases, editing, redrafting and finally producing a finished version of their work, it aims to get to the heart of the skills that most writers employ. Editing and re-drafting are more important while writing in a foreign language. The writing process is complex and recursive in nature, though focusing on the process may be time-consuming. The writing process is at least as important as the product.

subjective.question: What is brainstorming in the teaching of writing?
subjective.answer: Brainstorming is often a group exercise in which all students in the class are encouraged to participate by sharing their collective knowledge about a particular subject. It generates far more material than any one student thinks of on his/her own. Students can then utilize any or all of the information while preparing their first draft.

subjective.question: What is peer editing in the writing process?
subjective.answer: Peer editing is the stage of the writing process in which students exchange their rough drafts with classmates and give each other feedback on content, organization and language. It comes after the rough draft and before revising and final editing. It helps writers see their work from a reader's point of view, develops critical awareness, and makes revision purposeful.

subjective.question: What are integrated skills? Write a note on teaching through integrated skills.
subjective.answer: Integrated skills teaching involves teaching two or more of the four language skills (listening, speaking, reading, writing) together in a single lesson or activity, rather than in isolation. It reflects real-life language use, where skills are naturally combined — e.g. listening to a lecture and then discussing and writing about it. Two types of integrated-skill instruction are content-based instruction (theme-based, adjunct and sheltered models) and task-based instruction. Integration makes learning more meaningful, purposeful and communicative.

subjective.question: Define 'task' and write the types of tasks given by Willis (1996).
subjective.answer: A task is an activity in which learners use the target language to achieve a real outcome, with the focus on meaning rather than form. Willis (1996) lists these types of tasks: listing, ordering and sorting, comparing, problem solving, sharing personal experiences, and creative tasks. Other classifications include jigsaw tasks, information-gap tasks and decision-making tasks; tasks may also be one-way or two-way, convergent or divergent, collaborative or competitive, and involve simple or complex processing.

subjective.question: Define 'test'.
subjective.answer: A test, in simple terms, is a method of measuring a person's ability, knowledge, or performance in a given domain (Brown, 2004).

subjective.question: What are the types of assessment? Differentiate between formative and summative assessment.
subjective.answer: There are two main types of assessment. Formative assessment is carried out during the learning process; it is used to monitor students' learning and to provide feedback that improves teaching and learning. Summative assessment is carried out at the end of a course or term (e.g. final and midterm examinations) to evaluate and grade what students have achieved. In short, formative assessment is assessment FOR learning, while summative assessment is assessment OF learning.

subjective.question: Write the kinds of testing.
subjective.answer: The main kinds of testing are: (1) Placement tests — used to place students in a suitable level or group; (2) Diagnostic tests — used to identify learners' strengths and weaknesses; (3) Progress/achievement tests — used to measure what has been learnt from a course; (4) Proficiency tests — used to measure overall ability in the language regardless of any course; (5) Aptitude tests — used to predict a learner's future success in language learning; and (6) Language dominance tests — used to determine which of a bilingual's languages is stronger.

subjective.question: What are the steps involved in designing a language test?
subjective.answer: The steps in test design are: (1) define the purpose of the test — decide what the test is intended to measure; (2) set the objectives of the test; (3) draw up the test specifications — a broad outline of the test, what skills will be tested and what the items will be like; (4) devise the test tasks/items following the specifications; and (5) arrange grading or feedback. Item writers must be supplied with specifications and item-writing templates; the most problematic task is to ensure that the items meet the specifications.

subjective.question: Write the advantages of standardized tests.
subjective.answer: The advantages of standardized tests are: (1) they are a ready-made, previously validated product that frees the teacher from spending hours creating a test; (2) they can easily be administered to large groups within reasonable time limits; (3) their scoring procedures are streamlined; (4) they provide teachers with guidance for what and when something needs to be taught; (5) they are objective in nature; and (6) they provide accurate comparisons between subgroups.

subjective.question: What is portfolio assessment?
subjective.answer: Portfolio assessment is one of the most common alternatives in assessment. A portfolio is a purposeful collection of a student's work that shows effort, progress and achievement over time. It may include: essays and compositions in draft and final forms; reports and project outlines; poetry and creative prose; artwork, photos and newspaper or magazine clippings; audio and/or video recordings of presentations and demonstrations; journals, diaries and other personal reflections; tests, test scores and written homework exercises; and notes on lessons.

subjective.question: Write the common characteristics of alternatives in assessment.
subjective.answer: Alternatives in assessment: (1) use real-world contexts or simulations; (2) are non-intrusive, in that they extend day-to-day classroom activities; (3) allow students to be assessed on what they normally do in class; (4) use tasks that represent meaningful instructional activities; (5) focus on processes as well as products; (6) tap into higher-level thinking and problem-solving skills; (7) provide information about both the strengths and weaknesses of students; (8) are multi-culturally sensitive; (9) ensure that people, not machines, do the scoring, using human judgement; (10) encourage open disclosure of standards and rating criteria; and (11) call upon teachers to perform new instructional and assessment roles.

subjective.question: Differentiate between relative and absolute grading.
subjective.answer: In absolute grading, standards of performance are pre-specified on a numerical point system — for example, established points for a midterm test, points for a final exam, and points accumulated for the semester. In relative grading, students are ranked in the order of performance (percentile ranks) and grades are awarded relative to the group. Relative grading is more commonly used in many educational contexts, as it allows the teacher's own interpretation and adjustment for unpredicted ease or difficulty of a test.

subjective.question: What are the difficulties faced by learners in the classroom?
subjective.answer: The difficulties of learners depend upon how much their native language is different from English. Learners of English usually commit errors of grammar, vocabulary and pronunciation, because the structures, sound system and word stock of their mother tongue interfere with the target language. The greater the difference between L1 and English, the greater the learning difficulty is likely to be.

subjective.question: What is phonetics? Write its branches.
subjective.answer: Phonetics is the study of the nature of speech sounds themselves — it describes the articulatory and acoustic properties of phones (speech sounds) and studies which sounds are present in a language and how they can be represented using the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA). It has three branches: (1) Articulatory phonetics — the study of how speech sounds are made or articulated; (2) Acoustic phonetics — deals with the physical properties of speech sounds, such as sound waves in the air; (3) Auditory phonetics — deals with the perception of speech sounds via the ear.

subjective.question: Differentiate between phonetics and phonology.
subjective.answer: Phonetics is the study of the nature of sound itself: it describes the articulatory and acoustic properties of speech sounds, studies how the vocal tract apparatus modifies to produce recognizable speech sounds, and how sounds overlap in co-articulation. Phonology is the study of the sound system of a language: it studies how sounds interact as a system in a particular language, how they combine and change in combination, and which sounds can contrast to produce differences in meaning (described through distinctive features).

subjective.question: Write the place and manner of articulation of consonants.
subjective.answer: Place of articulation is the point in the vocal tract where the airflow is obstructed: bilabial (both lips, e.g. /p, b, m/), labiodental (lips and teeth, e.g. /f, v/), dental (tongue and teeth, e.g. /θ, ð/), alveolar (tongue and alveolar ridge, e.g. /t, d, s, z/), palatal (e.g. /ʃ, ʒ, tʃ, dʒ/), velar (back of tongue and soft palate, e.g. /k, g, ŋ/) and glottal (e.g. /h/). Manner of articulation is the nature of the obstruction: plosives/stops (complete closure, e.g. /p, t, k/), fricatives (narrowing causing friction, e.g. /f, s, ʃ/), affricates (stop + fricative, e.g. /tʃ, dʒ/), nasals (air through the nose, e.g. /m, n, ŋ/), and approximants (e.g. /w, j, r, l/). Consonants are commonly described by the VPM label: Voicing, Place and Manner.

subjective.question: What are voiced and voiceless sounds? Give examples.
subjective.answer: Sounds produced with vibration of the vocal folds are called voiced sounds, e.g. the sound of [z] in the word 'hazy' — you can feel the vibration if you put your fingers to your larynx and produce [z]. The sounds which are produced without such vibration are called voiceless sounds, e.g. the sound of [s] in the word 'miss'.

subjective.question: What is morphology? Define morpheme and its kinds.
subjective.answer: Morphology is the study of the internal structure of words — how words are formed from smaller meaningful units. A morpheme is the smallest meaningful unit of language. Kinds of morphemes: (1) Free morphemes — can stand alone as words (e.g. 'book'); (2) Bound morphemes — cannot stand alone and must attach to other forms (e.g. '-ness'); (3) Lexical/content morphemes — carry the content of the message (nouns, verbs, adjectives); (4) Functional morphemes — serve grammatical functions (articles, prepositions, conjunctions); (5) Derivational morphemes — used to make new words (e.g. '-ness', 're-'); (6) Inflectional morphemes — indicate grammatical functions such as tense, number and possession (e.g. '-s', '-ed'). A variation of a morpheme is called an allomorph.

subjective.question: Define 'lexeme' and 'lexicon'.
subjective.answer: A lexeme is the fundamental unit of the lexicon — an abstract vocabulary item that represents all the inflected forms a word can take; for example, 'go', 'goes', 'went' and 'gone' are forms of the single lexeme GO. The lexicon is the vocabulary of a language — the total stock of words and lexical items a language has, together with the information stored about them in the speaker's mind (their form, meaning and use).

subjective.question: What is blending as a word-formation process? Give examples.
subjective.answer: Blending is the combination of two separate forms to produce a single new term, typically by taking only the beginning of one word and joining it to the end of the other word. Examples: smoke + fog = smog; smoke + haze = smaze; binary + digit = bit; breakfast + lunch = brunch; motor + hotel = motel. Blends are common in the media, e.g. telecast, telethon, infotainment, and in the mixing of languages, e.g. Spanglish (Spanish/English). In a few blends we combine the beginnings of both words, e.g. modem (modulator/demodulator).

subjective.question: What is borrowing as a word-formation process? Give examples.
subjective.answer: Borrowing is the taking over of words from other languages. It is one of the most common sources of new words in English. Throughout its history, English has adopted a vast number of words from other languages: croissant (French), dope (Dutch), piano (Italian), pretzel (German), sofa (Arabic), tycoon (Japanese) and yogurt (Turkish). Other languages also borrow terms from English, as in the Japanese use of 'suupaamaaketto' (supermarket). A special type of borrowing is loan-translation or calque — a direct translation of the elements of a word into the borrowing language, e.g. 'aeroplane' (hawai jahaz in Urdu).

subjective.question: What are eponyms? Give examples.
subjective.answer: Eponyms are new words formed from the names of people or places, where the word's meaning is derived from that person or place. Examples include 'sandwich' (from the Earl of Sandwich), 'boycott' (from Captain Boycott), 'jeans' (from Genoa) and 'denim' (from Nîmes, France).

subjective.question: What is a constituent? Write its types.
subjective.answer: A constituent is 'a syntactic unit that functions as part of a larger unit within a sentence'. A constituent can be a word, phrase, clause or a sentence, but it will function as a complete unit (Meyer, 2009). Constituency is at the centre of any discussion of syntax: syntactic units are not simply arbitrarily grouped and ordered, but form identifiable units. Syntacticians have identified four different levels of structure at which constituents occur: sentences → clauses → phrases → words. There are two types of constituents: immediate constituents — the separate units into which a given structure can be divided at a particular level (e.g. subject and predicate in a sentence) — and ultimate constituents, the smallest units obtained at the final level of division.

subjective.question: Differentiate between modifiers and complements in a sentence.
subjective.answer: Complements are elements that are required to complete the meaning of a head word or a sentence — for example, in 'She is a teacher', 'a teacher' is a complement of the verb 'is', and removing it makes the sentence incomplete. Modifiers are optional elements that add extra information about a head word but are not required for the sentence to be complete — for example, in 'She is an excellent teacher', 'excellent' modifies 'teacher' and can be removed without making the sentence ungrammatical. In short, complements are obligatory and closely bound to the head, while modifiers are optional and descriptive.

subjective.question: Differentiate between semantics and semiotics.
subjective.answer: Semantics is the study of meaning in language — how words, phrases and sentences carry meaning, including reference, sense and lexical relations. Semiotics is the broader study of signs and sign systems in general, of which linguistic meaning is only one part. Signs are of three types: iconic signs, which physically resemble what they stand for (e.g. a picture); indexical signs, which are related to some sensory feature (e.g. smoke signifies fire); and symbolic signs, which have no natural relation with what they refer to (e.g. words).

subjective.question: Write a note on the mentalistic (cognitive/conceptual) theory of meaning.
subjective.answer: The mentalistic, cognitive or conceptual theory of meaning holds that the meaning of a word or expression is the idea, concept or mental image it evokes in the mind of the speaker and the hearer. On this view, words are symbols that stand for concepts formed in the mind on the basis of experience; to understand a word is to have the corresponding concept. The theory is criticized because concepts are private and may differ from person to person, so it cannot fully explain how meaning is shared and stable in communication.

subjective.question: Define synonyms and antonyms with examples.
subjective.answer: Synonyms are words with very closely related or similar meanings; they can often, though not always, be substituted for each other — e.g. we can say 'What was his answer?' or 'What was his reply?' with much the same meaning. Other examples: almost/nearly, big/large, broad/wide, buy/purchase, cab/taxi, car/automobile, couch/sofa, freedom/liberty. Antonyms are words that are opposite in meaning. Simple (non-gradable/complementary) antonyms are pairs such that the negative of one implies the positive of the other, e.g. dead/alive, pass/fail, hit/miss, male/female.

subjective.question: What is evidentiality? Write its types.
subjective.answer: Evidentiality is the grammatical marking of the source of information for what is said — how the speaker knows what he/she claims. Its types are: (1) Witness evidentiality — the speaker witnessed the event; (2) Sensory evidentiality — the information comes through the senses; (3) Inferential evidentiality — the information is inferred from evidence; (4) Reportative evidentiality — the information is reported by someone else; (5) Assumed evidentiality — the information is assumed to be the case.

subjective.question: Differentiate between semantics and pragmatics.
subjective.answer: Semantics is the study of the literal, context-independent meaning of words and sentences — what expressions mean by themselves. Pragmatics is the study of what speakers mean — how meaning depends on the context, the speaker's intention and the hearer's interpretation, including deixis, reference, presupposition, implicature and speech acts. In short, semantics studies sentence meaning, while pragmatics studies speaker meaning in use.

subjective.question: What is the role of a teacher as a 'prompter' in intensive reading?
subjective.answer: In intensive reading, the teacher's role as a prompter is to nudge and encourage students while they work closely with a text: prompting them to notice particular features of the text (such as vocabulary, structures or the writer's purpose), to re-read a segment for detail, and to check their understanding, without simply giving them the answers. The prompter supports learners at the moment of difficulty so that they can extract the detailed meaning themselves.

subjective.question: Write any three principles of teaching English.
subjective.answer: Three basic principles of teaching English are: (1) Learner-centredness — teaching should focus on the learners' needs, levels and interests, not only on the teacher and the textbook. (2) Meaningful communication — learners should use English for real communication and meaningful tasks, not only memorize rules and word lists. (3) Gradual, supported progression — language should be presented in manageable steps from simple to complex, with plenty of practice, feedback and opportunities to use the language in and beyond the classroom.

subjective.question: Write a note on the spread of English around the world.
subjective.answer: English spread around the world mainly through British colonization: it was carried to America, Australia, New Zealand, Canada and South Africa by settlers (the Inner Circle), and imposed as the language of administration and education in colonies in Asia and Africa (the Outer Circle). In the twentieth century its spread was accelerated by the global influence of the United States in trade, science, technology, media and popular culture, so that countries with no colonial link to English began teaching it as the principal foreign language (the Expanding Circle). Today its special role is recognized by almost every country, either by making it an official language or by requiring its study as a foreign language.

subjective.question: Write the advantages of using audio-visual aids in language teaching.
subjective.answer: The advantages of audio-visual aids are: (1) they make the teaching-learning process vivid and concrete, so learners understand and retain language better; (2) they present authentic models of pronunciation, stress and intonation for listening and imitation; (3) they arouse learners' interest and motivation and break the monotony of textbook teaching; (4) they provide meaningful context for new vocabulary and structures through pictures, films and recordings; and (5) they cater to different learning styles, especially visual and auditory learners.

subjective.question: What is Kachru's Expanding Circle? Give examples.
subjective.answer: The Expanding Circle is the third of Kachru's three concentric circles of English. It includes countries where English has no historical or official role and is learnt as a foreign language (EFL) for international communication; these countries are norm-dependent, looking to the Inner Circle for norms. Examples include China, Egypt, Indonesia, Israel, Japan, Korea, Nepal, Saudi Arabia, Taiwan and Russia.

subjective.question: Write the criticism of the notion of 'methods' that led to the post-method era.
subjective.answer: The notion of methods came under criticism in the 1990s, and the term 'post-method era' came into use. The main criticisms are: methods typically prescribe for teachers what and how to teach; good teaching is regarded as the correct use of the method; the role of the teacher is marginalized — moreover, learners are viewed as passive recipients of the method who must submit to its regime of exercises and activities; the concept of learner-centredness and teacher creativity remains absent; and methods remain less flexible and adaptive to learners' needs and interests. Mainstream language teaching therefore no longer regards methods as the key factor in accounting for success or failure in language teaching.
